utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I'd like to briefly deal with scheduling. The Chamber is aware of the positions of the parties, it being that considerable time will be needed for cross-examination and that even Friday in the afternoon, sitting in the afternoon, would not help you out. The Chamber has considered this. Mr. Waespi, if you would take another hour, then that would mean that we would -- when we would also sit Friday in the afternoon, we would have 13 hours left altogether and I'm talking about effective examination time. If you'd just take the net hours, I mean, a sitting day is four hours and 45 minutes, 45 minutes of break, that makes four hours, and my calculations for 13 hours, I started at three and a half hours for a day session, which would mean that for Wednesday, Thursday, Friday morning, Friday afternoon, we'd have all together 14 hours minus one hour to be taken by Mr. Waespi today. That's 13 hours. The Chamber considers that it should be possible to at least give it a serious try to finish the case, and therefore, suggest to the Defence teams to agree on how they would -- how they would use 11 hours for cross-examination. We would then still have a couple -- two hours left, perhaps re-examination, perhaps some questions from the Bench. Let's see, whether, in the total of 13 hours remaining after Mr. Waespi has finished his examination-in-chief, whether we can achieve that. The Chamber is aware, especially in the circumstances, where reference was made to Rule 91 at an early stage, that the Chamber will adapt the schedule, if it appears that, that would be required by the fairness of the trial, which should be guaranteed by the Chamber. That remains unaffected. Nevertheless, 13 hours, let's see whether we can do it. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand your instruction completely and I know you're aware of this but I feel the need to make a record on our behalf concerning the time. We feel strongly that I will certainly try to get that done within the time you have allotted. However, we feel strongly given the fact that we have five witness statements here, there will be approximately five to six hours worth of direct testimony, there are 20 to 30 sitreps, and 100-day report, that time should be given to the defendants in particular, because we are not talking about one or two topic areas, if I may use an expression, the kitchen sink here in this -- through this witness has been thrown at us, and it will take some time to cover each topic with this witness. Given that, I completely understand the Trial Chamber's desire and, as always, will strive to make the cross-examination as effective as possible dealing with the issues. However, did I want to state that we feel very strongly concerning this witness and that we be given the amount of time necessary to do a proper and thorough job in the cross-examination. And as I said, I'm sure that the Trial Chamber was already aware of that but I wanted to make that clear on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You already started speaking more quickly in order to achieve that. Mr. Waespi, you have until quarter past 3.00, I would say. You said four and a half hours. You've taken three hours and 45 minutes. This would bring you -- and if you would take five minutes more, that is already part of our calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony, and I do understand that although you have travel arrangements that that would be only for later on Friday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have been corresponding with the Prosecutor and arranged that my latest departure from The Hague would be Friday evening. I have a prime minister's visit to attend to and I simply have to leave The Hague on Friday evening. I am, however, of course in the interests of justice, prepared to reappear here or produce material in writing or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: An afternoon session goes, then, till 7.00 p.m., that would be still --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your plane leaves at what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Hmm. That creates an additional problem. Let's get started and see whether Mr. Waespi has a private plane for you. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Since the previous Prosecutor has left there is no more government plane available to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can understand that you're suffering, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to clarify. I assume that the witness meant he has been contacting through the Victim and Witnesses Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether the correspondence, Mr. Waespi, was -- first of all, it was in writing. It was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Prior to the witness being sworn in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If 65 ter 5441 could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Liborius, while that is being done, did you maintain a notebook, a patrol notebook while you were on mission in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that notebook?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to record observations and informations, statements and the like that I observed during my monitoring activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, please have a look at this document. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a meeting conducted on the 19th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you first. What is it -- have you prepared this document, before you go into the contents?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did you prepare it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prepared it the day before yesterday or so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to page 3 of this document. And the basis for this document was what, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis is my patrol notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe we need to go to the next page. Yes. Can you tell us what it says under the entry of the 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Danish or in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voting in barracks. 4 Guards Brigade, under General Gotovina, arrow, Guards Brigade commander, arrow, Ministry of Defence, soldiers will vote in barracks. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. Let me ask you, do you remember having met with General Gotovina on or about 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the preparations of the elections we had a host of meetings with different authorities in that period, and in and around that time, yes, a short meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how do you remember that you had a short meeting with General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was decided that that -- the further detailed discussions should be delegated to some of the aides in his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of the aide in Mr. Gotovina's staff?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall his function?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written on the yellow Post-It note that is referred to a little bit down below. Colonel Seric, Deputy Commander OZ Split, for political affairs. He later introduced himself as an aide to General Gotovina during that meeting that was held on the 26th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If this piece could be admitted into evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see and hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P821 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let move to the 27th of October. And I would like to have 65 ter 4337 brought up, please. Now do you know who Colonel or General Gambotti was, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. He was the designated Head of Regional Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of what organisation?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now are you familiar with this document that you see on your screen now, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you the drafter?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On the bottom part of the document, we see reference to a meeting between the HRC DES with the OZ Split commander General Gotovina. Does that refer to Mr. Gambotti?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The HRC designate is Mr. Gambotti.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it goes on to the next page, if we could see that, please. Is that an accurate representation of what occurred during the meeting in your memory, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a condensed and accurate version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And before drafting and indeed filing this report, I take it it has been filed ultimately. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. ECMM reports were sent and filed in the headquarters of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Before doing that, did you discuss the contents of what you wrote down in relation to that meeting with General Gotovina and Mr. Gambotti, with Mr. Gambotti?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed the meetings we had throughout the day and also, of course, the one we had with General Gotovina. It was indeed a long one and HRC designate Gambotti and I discussed in details the way the meeting went before I drafted that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On what basis did you draft this report? Did you have notes which would have helped you drafting the report?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several pages, yes. And the HRC designate's own impressions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this document could be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P822.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P822 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Waespi, the previous exhibit is partly in Danish, partly in English. How would you expect the Chamber to -- to digest that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. We instructed an outside service to make a translation, verbatim translation of the Danish parts and we will receive it shortly. So I hope tomorrow morning we will have it for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I then put on the record that, of course, the admission is conditional to receiving a full English text. Now, these apparently are notes, may I take it handwritten notes, the original seems not to be attached to it. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel a need to step in here. We have been produced his entire notebook and an entire diary and I will work it out with Mr. Waespi but we believe and we'll tender both in their entirety in the cross-examination. I will work out with him whose going to pay for the translation but actually we'll have both translated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At the end, we all have the same UN background as it comes to translation services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the optimistic view on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's move to 65 ter 5434.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Liborius, can you tell us what you see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you specify which parts of your notebook?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my second notebook and it covers the dates for 27 October -- yeah. Both pages, I have the notebook at my availability here for the Chamber, if that serves in their interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the right side, do you see a reference to the meeting we were just discussing with you, General Gotovina and Mr. Gambotti?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is it indeed the first page of the many pages of notes I took during the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go slowly through the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the next page could be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that the next sequence?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You see the questions discussed. They are in numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, up until -- I should state that if I am required to relate and reflect and reproduce what is in the notes I must suggest that I have the notebook in front of me. It's in my bag. Because it is not really so clearly visible here on the screen. Have I seen a photocopy of it. It is much more clear on a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The only purpose is to identify that this is a true copy of what you have in your notebook and we do have another exhibit, a typewritten version of this notebook. If we can move on to the last page, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, Mr. Waespi. Is this the same notebook or a different notebook from which we got the transcript in the previous -- one of the previous exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It is the same one from the -- the same series of notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this is the last page. Can you confirm that, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And in the interests of saving time, Your Honour, I am prepared to produce the notebook so that the Judges can have it in front of them. Under the condition that I receive it -- return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If this would not find any objection with the Defence counsel, then of course we could have a look at the notebook.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the usher please assist in ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This the first one; this is the second one; this is the one we're looking at now, the small one; and the first one covers the previous month. They are my property. Your Honour, you should look at the yellow mark in the little book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find our way through it, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would note that if there is it a colour distinction or things like that in the notebook, we haven't been produced anything in colour. So, I don't know what -- oh, I see, Post-It notes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If this could receive an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P823 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now in producing those notes, who did you do that? Did you take them at the meeting or after the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the meeting as it was in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How good of a note-taker are you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a fairly senior civil servant in the Danish administration. I would suggest that my note takings have been trained and refined over a couple of years. My prime minister relies on them, and will in a few days' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius. If we could go back to 5441, please; that's the Exhibit we discussed at the outset of today. And if we could move to page 5, please. In front of you, do you see now a typed written version of your notes as it relates to that meeting of the 27th of October?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I produced it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move to item 15, which is at the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we can go back, please. Yes. Item 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, using these notes here and your memory, can you let us, what was discussed under item 15?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It dealt with the question of what would happen if a military operation occurred in Sector East. How would the Croatian forces be controlled. Prior to the item 15 had been a discussion of the tactical manuals for increasing control. That had been the topic of the -- that section of the conversation. The conversation had reached, I would say, a very -- the atmosphere was good, it was tense, it was a give-and-take conversation between Gambotti and General Gotovina. The first sentence, [Foreign language spoken], if a military operation comes, how will the HV forces be controlled, was the question raised by Gambotti. And then follows the answer by General Gotovina. It had been the subject prior 13, 12, 13, 14, the NCO corps. The availability of them and the possibility for them for exercising control in the military rank and the General focussed on the fact that they lacked the sufficiently trained and skilled NCOs giving, among others, the -- the result -- that was a result of the years under Marshal Tito, the Yugoslav whole mentality, the way the armed forces were structured. The fact that the NCOs -- some of them had also had bad experiences. They were amongst all the people who were expelled from the Krajina-held areas, that the feeling of harassment that they felt, that that taken in total produced an environment in which the appropriate professional execution of a NCO function as a controlling and commanding element in the chain of command was not properly working. However, the General stated that the professional soldiers were of a higher quality. Then the conversation ping-ponged forward and at a certain point General Gotovina -- Gambotti, HRC designate Gambotti asked the question whether, okay, we have discussed NCOs and the way they can exercise their command but we all know that extraordinary events took place and the General concurred in that. And then at that time, the silence kicked in to that part of the conversation, because at that time it was, well, admitted that extraordinary events did -- occurred at a quite a large-scale and that the previous, so to speak, protection of the integrity of the NCO corps and the developments trying to keep the professional soldiers out responsibility of that has, so to speak, been eroded. The conversation was conducted through silence, I would say. And that was a distinct change in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wish to note that the document on the screen was prepared by the witness a few days ago. I have now noticed that he transcribed his notes, it says in 15: "Professional soldiers." And in his original notebook it says: "Professional soldiers were controlled." The two words "were controlled" are omitted from what Mr. Liborius put on the paper here. Just for the record, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we could reproduce the notebook itself, it is perhaps easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about 15. Under 15, prof soldiers, is that the portion --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and the next words are "were controlled," in the original that I have been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have the page in front of me. That's the page with the pyramid on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to look at it. Could you perhaps provide me with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 65 ter number would be 5434.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is what I was produced by the Office of the Prosecutor, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see whether that looks more or less like the original I have got here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It would be the last page in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we have it now on our screen. What is missing in your version?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Nothing it missing in my version. What was written before -- on the document before was purported to be a transcript of this and what I'm pointing out is that when Mr. Liborius prepared this transcript, he put "professional soldiers" and then the sentence "were controlled" is omitted from the transcript that he has prepared. The typed version that was on our screen a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what is on our screen, what line do I find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is now the notebook which is P -- P821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second. I think a whole line is missing not only "were controlled," but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Much improved, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to an error in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the reason, Your Honour, that I would prefer to refer to my written notes because those are in front of you, and if we can relate to that I would feel more confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the issue dealing with at this moment could be produced on your screen. I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's perfect for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can see it on your screen at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the portion we are talking about, you'll see that the words "were controlled" and then the "D," and then something that's difficult to read for me, "improved," do not appear on your transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The meeting at that time had gone on for some -- I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is just a transcript error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let's take the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On that basis I'd ask, Your Honour, that the P -- P823 be marked for identification until we can make sure that everything has been transcribed properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And of course it is a selection of the notebook anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But even that selection should reflect what is actually in the notebook at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, there is no doubt about that. Then we will have if marked for identification for the time being until the portions transcribed have been fully checked. How much time would you need for that Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Given that I'm doing the cross-examination, Your Honour, should we do it while the witness is still here, or I would prefer to do it early next week -- to get back to you early next week, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll get a translation later today and so I can disclose it to Defence and we have an English translation of everything that is in Danish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps other counsel may be just as much interested. Someone has just to check it. It's as simple as that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now earlier, Mr. Liborius, you said that it was admitted that extraordinary events occurred, I believe. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What happened between the line "professional soldiers were controlled though much improved," and then "extraordinary" on one line was that the ping-pong between General Gotovina and Mr. Gambotti, narrowed in the -- the focus of the conversation into how was the control exercised over, not only reserve units but also professional units. The starting point of General Gotovina's explanation was that professional soldiers were controlled, were completely free of accusations of having engaged in irregular activities burning and looting and that stuff, and as the discussion in 15 developed to a crucial point where -- that is where "extraordinary," that word, is reflecting there, had reached such a tense atmosphere. Now I want you to remember that the two persons had in -- had a tete-a-tete before the formal meeting started. They were speaking French.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And by the two persons you mean?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gotovina and Gambotti, who was a senior French officer. So there was a good rapport between the two gentlemen. Gambotti being a senior, old, experienced French officer and the General having a good rapport with him. So you may say that it was difficult to escape the subject and just giving lip service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And therefore, as the conversation became more focussed on, well, there was these extraordinary events, yes, they were there, was the silent admittance. I, as a note-taker, would not be -- keep -- working with my pencil because it would seriously disturb the rapport between the two gentlemen. It is not like, you know, you sit in the school and take dictation. And we both interpreted that the silence there was -- the silence by General Gotovina was, in fact, the answer. It was an a silent exception that, yes, extraordinary events did take place and the soldiers that General Gotovina -- Colonel Gambotti mentioned had indeed taken part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what is meant by extraordinary events?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Burning and looting mainly. But extraordinary events was at that time the common phrase used by the Croatian government and Croatian officials for all sorts of activities that -- that included killing, burning, looting, extraordinary events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you mentioned a couple of times NCO corps or NCOs. What are NCOs?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the middle level commanders, sergeants and that stuff. The level of soldiers that are so crucial in controlling the men in your unit. Can you be a fine general, you can be a fine officer, but you need the NCOs, the sergeants, in order to maintain control of your field units --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the five to 15 unit size. And if I may relate to what I said yesterday, when you do see a unit of say five to fifteen soldiers moving around they will usually in their -- down to earth business, be controlled by the NCOs. And if the NCOs do not react or act in a proper way, they accept killing, burning, looting, whatever, then the entire morale in the unit simply is eroded very fast. I can say that as a previous soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me move on to item 16 on the same last page. Can you tell us what was discussed?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 16 and 17, [Foreign language spoken] translates into who has been arrested. A question by Gambotti. The reply from General Gotovina was that General Cermak would have that information and he would continue with some details there. But in general, the situation was okay. Saying that well, okay, some people have perhaps been doing these extraordinary events, discussed in 15, but in general the situation is under control, it's okay. And he continues: There are [Foreign language spoken] extraordinary events. There is always extraordinary events, a repetition of the 15 [Foreign language spoken] I don't have concrete information. So the General flips between being, if you wish, honest with the senior French officer that he has established a good rapport with and, on the other hand, keeping the official line. That is the art of the -- the conversation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether we have this document admitted already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the document was admitted but the transcription is now marked for identification, the selected portions. Could I ask one question. In 16, we find the word "events." Has that word been there when you wrote it or has it been changed at any later stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly not. What you see in front of you is what was produced in that meeting. And I can assure you under oath that the diary and what you see in front of you is what was produced at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, everything you say is under oath, so therefore that needs -- it's not specific for this answer. Could I -- you rightly said that this is your property. Could I nevertheless instruct you that should keep it so that the original is -- will always be available when needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour. I don't know whether Your Honour is finished looking at the document, might the Defence bar have a look at it as well in the original form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original. I take it that there's no objection against temporarily leaving it and I take it that the Defence, certainly in view of the instructions I just gave, has no concern to give it back to you once they've inspected it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to meetings you had with General Cermak. How many times did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With General Cermak, I don't have the exact number. From time to time we would meet to discuss different issues of running the ECMM operation. We would sometimes discuss human rights -- humanitarian issues. I would have some of the meetings, my humanitarian officer would have some. So from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to 65 ter 4002. This is a daily report of 5th August, and it refers to the fact that the new military governor is General Cermak. I'm sure we will see it in a moment. Now, that's the 5th of August, a report by you. Was that the first time you heard of Mr. Cermak and the fact that he is the military governor?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have it enlarged, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why do you describe him as military governor in this report?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at that time we had information via UN and I believe also public media that a new general had been installed in Knin as a military governor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now in the meetings you were present, how was he addressed, as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either as General Cermak or the military governor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, did he ever protest as to the fact that you called him military governor?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn to your second witness statement. That's P800. At page 3, where you say that, and I quote: "Turning to the authority of General Cermak, the military governor, there is reason to say that his authority grew during the month of August and September." And then you move on to discuss the rising authority in relation to how you got through check-points. Do you have other examples of how you saw his authority increasing?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we discussed yesterday, frequently a -- a call to him or his staff would resolve a restriction of movement problems. And as the weeks progressed after Operation Storm, sometimes the mentioning of his name would suffice to -- to solve the problems of restriction of movements or in conversation with soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In general, based on the meetings you had with him and perhaps other people, how did you see his authority?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw General Cermak's authority indeed as military governor. The senior figure in charge of the, you may say, housekeeping, not the operational military figure. And his words to me was that he was sent to ensure the upholding of law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could move back to 65 ter 5441. And I do apologise that it might be exhibits already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And does it refer to a meeting you had with General Cermak on the 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting between General Cermak and a visiting troika delegation of EU ambassadors, France, Spain and Italy, I believe, and I participated in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now I see that there are subject matters that were discussed. Was the issue of burning and destruction raised during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. If I am to relate to the meeting, I again prefer that my notebook is produced on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can move on, what we have on the screen, the next page -- or perhaps also it would be fair to have temporarily the notebook given to the witness so he could refer to it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's the 19 October 1995.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you let us know what was said in relation to the issue of burning and destruction.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the meetings -- throughout the meeting, in the different questions, burning and destruction was an element. In the first question of the Spanish ambassador where, as a first, he dwelled on the humanitarian problems, the reply of General Cermak was to contain that denial of -- of that. That is carried in the word [Foreign language spoken]. We should move up on the page. We have the second page in front of us, in the printed version. Secondly, in the questions of the French ambassador, now we are on that page we have on the screen, later in the meeting where he returned to the -- the French ambassador returned to the subject specifically asking why Kistanje was burnt. FRA AMB is French ambassador. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can we go back to the page we just had on the screen.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: FRA AMB is French ambassador asking Kistanje question, why being burned, why burned. General Cermak answered, Well, happened during Operation Storm and the day after. Professional army is okay, but reserve units and Home Guard, they are just people. The notes reflect the statements by General Cermak that Kistanje was burned during Operation Storm and just the day after. That he then continued on saying that it was not the responsibility of the professional army but the Kistanje had been burned by reserve units or Home Guards and as they are just simple people, i.e., they act out of revenge, they are wanting to -- to repay for all the harassment that they have suffered and the issues we discussed during the Gotovina meeting, the motivation for that. If I may, Your Honour, refer to the discussion I produced in the report for the visiting senators where I would said that I would, in that report, produce input for the discussion. These were the elements that were usually produced during discussions on what happened and who were engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius. Just one more question on this page. Security of Serbs, what was discussed? Just below the entry you see on the screen, Varivode.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The question was raised by the French ambassador, what about the security of the Serbs? General Cermak replied, We have increased the police presence. There are, of course, scattered hamlets. They are far away, difficult to -- to come around in. Of course we know that as the winter will start, we will see that -- that will mean problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Liborius. Let me move in the remaining few minutes, very briefly to two subjects. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic. Is there anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting, patiently, Your Honour, until now, but I thought that 3.15 -- is it one hour or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We started a bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Like the Defence, I have to cover a number of topics because the evidence requires it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may respond, I only have eight hours, you've had much more than that with the statements. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 65 ter 4359, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You -- I think it has been mentioned already that you drafted a special report dated 26 November 1995, entitled: 100 days after Operation Storm in the former Serb Krajina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review it before you came to testify?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And is it an accurate description of what you observed, what other people told you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to have the report admitted, Mr. President, once it comes on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections? Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a lengthy report, so it may take some time to have it brought up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P824.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P824, in the absence of any objection, is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last point is -- I'd like to refer you to your first witness statement, 1995, now P799. In the middle of the last page - it's your first witness statement - middle of the last page: "HV MP and CRO POL personnel. My assessment of the number of the police was that it fitted the requirement needed to control civilians, POWs and others in a sustained period of combat operations. They were everywhere. In the Knin town and outside and in the rest of Sector South, the personnel to control the whole sector was in place." Do you stand by this?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just, Mr. President, before I forget, of course we have filed a 92 ter motion which has a few documents I haven't addressed but they are in the witness statements addressed which are now in evidence and a few photographs also addressed in the witness statements so I would like to move these into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They were attached to the statement or were they just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: They were just mentioned in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have no -- I can't reproduce at this moment an exact list. Could you please produce a short list in which we find what has not yet been dealt with so that we can then ask the Defence whether there are any objections to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your net time finally was four hours and 33 minutes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Misetic, will you be the first to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for the Prosecution -- for Mr. Gotovina. I am -- I apologise. Gives me an opportunity, Mr. Misetic, to point at a small mistake you made earlier, when you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's impossible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- P823 be marked for identification whereas you apparently wanted the transcript to be marked for identification which is P821.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your mistake is minor. Mine is not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, first, I noticed when you came and sat in the chair you immediately wanted to take notes and can I ask you why you needed to take notes?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I know that you would ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Ask you what?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do take notes in my profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Something you -- it's standard practice for you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it's important for me, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. In your diary, you make reference so something called Dan Del. You had to prepare a report for Dan Del. Do you know what Dan Del stands for?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Danish delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what Danish delegation you were referring?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Danish delegation of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in that same diary entry you will recall it says you are writing a report for UMN as part of the Dan Del monthly report. Can you tell us what UMN stand for?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stands for Unres Ministaire [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And can you -- in English, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Of which country?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Denmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And -- thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic and Mr. Liborius, you are developing a speed which is almost impossible to follow for transcribing what you say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Madam Registrar, if I could have P801, please. If we could go to page 7 in the English version, please. And go to the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to start by reading you that bottom paragraph of your statement from 2005, Mr. Liborius. "I had met Gotovina previously in his office in Knin sometime in August 1995. I don't remember the exact date. When I protested about the fact that Gotovina wanted us to give up our premises in Knin, as they were required for Croatian soldiers and that he had reserved for his own purposes the large ECMM building. I refused to give in, and he then said that ECMM must therefore leave Knin. I argued that the Croatian government would not be complying with its own obligations that the president had signed up to. This angered Gotovina and he stormed out. The Croatian Senior Liaison Officer, I cannot recall his name, he was bearded, told me that I was crazy to have responded in this manner, as Gotovina, held life and death in his hands." Now my first question to you, Mr. Liborius, is: It's true, is it not, that that never happened. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you, sorry there's a noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There apparently was a -- a problem. I also heard something not normal in my earphones. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm trying to listen to the French in order to keep on pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, my question and I will repeat it from the transcript, it's true, is it not, that that never happened what you described there in your witness statement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's true that you never had a meeting or a conversation with General Gotovina where you had an argument with him about the ECMM premises and the Croatian government taking it over and then subsequent to that meeting that the CALO, the Croatian Army Liaison Officer, told you that were crazy to have responded in this manner and that Gotovina held life and death in his hands. That never happened, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I had a meeting with him and he stormed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You're a good note taker and the prime minister relies on your notes so could you look in your notebook, please, and point out the specific passage where the commander of the Split Military District had an argument with you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And let me take that back. This statement by the CALO that were crazy to have responded in this manner as Gotovina held life and death in his hands, that could be perceived as a threat to your physical security, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Lukovic was a generally --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- kind man so I did not consider that as a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You didn't consider that Colonel Lukovic telling you that General Gotovina held life and death in his hands --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was right after the General had stormed out that I must have been crazy. He said that with half a smile or that -- that I should not have responded that way, that I had to move from the ECMM accommodation and that of course the -- the words of the General were law as he held life and death in his hands. I did not consider that as a personal threat to my security at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: So this was kind of a half-hearted, sort of joking statement by the CALO, is that it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will have to ask him, sir, whether it was a joke. It was a part of the housekeeping business where the ECMM could have its office and its accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a subject that we discussed in numerous conversations throughout August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, sorry to cut you off but I need to get through as many factual --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I understand, Mr. Waespi, I will allow him to answer factually but given the constrictions on time, I am going to try and get him focussed on specific answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, could you please try to focus your answers very much on the precise questions. If Mr. Misetic wants further details, he will certainly ask you for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, it caught my attention, obviously, that the prime minister depends on your notes so if you could please refer to your notebook or your diary or if you know of a daily report where you reported this incident with General Gotovina and then we can proceed from there to discuss those parts of your notes, diary, or the daily report.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue, as I said, was an ongoing one, so in that case, I did not have to take notes in my diary for that and my diary served another purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You had to take notes when you sat down in this chair, but you never wrote down anywhere, am I right, of this type of incident of General Gotovina and the CALO; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did in my notebook once, I recall, had an entry on the accommodation and office issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is true. And we'll take a look at that right now. However, you have looked at your notebook and you know that there is no reference to a meeting with General Gotovina there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to this issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's right. Okay. Well, let's take a look at your diary, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 1D50-0069. Sorry, I'll call up the first page number which is 1D50-0001. And now if we could move to 0069, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm -- sorry. Mr. Liborius, I'm going to read you three entries at the same time in the interests of saving time, and then I will ask you a few questions. This is your entry for the 2nd of September --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prefer to relate to my original notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. This is -- however, it has been stipulated by the Prosecution that you actually have gone through this document reviewed it, made corrections to it and returned it back to the Office of the Prosecutor as an accurate representation of your diary. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm asked a question with regard to my notebook, I would like to refer to my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm just asking you to -- is it correct that this transcript of your diary, not your notebook, is accurate because you were the one who received it, the original draft, you made corrections to it and then returned it back to the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in all human activity there is a slight risk of small error, so if I'm asked to relate to what I wrote, I would like to refer to it and I have it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. You can use your diary; I'm going to use what is on the screen. Because that is it all I have.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are working on the basis of the material which is uploaded in the e-court system. If there's any reason at any moment to have any doubt as to whether that is not a true copy of the original, then please draw my attention to that, and then we'll see whether we -- we have to verify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you can't read it as it is reproduced --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is 00 -- yeah, good, it's the 2nd of September in the original. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You'll see there, sir, it says you entered in your diary: "Today we are moving the rest of the Knin office. I am going to a meeting with the CALOs. Kreso, Stanko and Karolj are there." Do you recall the CALOs, sir, as Stanko Bacic, Kreso Dragic and Karolj Dondo? Do those names mean anything do you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dondo does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Bacic or Dragic?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was their first names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Kreso Dragic and Stanko Bacic. Do you recall them as being the CALOs?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanko Babic, yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "I come informally, casually, by and tell them that we have found a good place. Chief of police office is aware of it and that it suits our needs." Then skipping some sentences: "NATO planes are bombing BSA positions again," that would be Bosnian Serb army. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "The CRO can hardly hide their enthusiasm for this. They feel like they are almost in the same club as us. But no, dear friends, you and not members of the EU, WEU, NATO, or the European Council. You have committed far too many war crimes for that." If we could turn the page, please, two pages. For 6 September, again: "Meeting with CALOs about accommodations for ECMM. I refuse to move because a General has gotten the idea to move into our earliest RC Knin house. They are offering to find something else for us. I'd really like to see that but everything turns out, as expected, to be a pile of shit." Then you go on down towards the middle of that: "Then I will close the Knin office and report that ECMM work is not welcome in this lawless country so they can expect to say farewell to DEM and FHARE," et cetera, et cetera. And then if we can go to the 7th of September. Beginning part of this so I don't spend a lot of time reading it out, you went to the RC building in Knin. "The stench reaches all the way up to the top floor. It seems as if it is destiny. After the property has been taken over, the reek of cadavers and dog corpses is foul and hangs in the walls. Here you go, General Gotovina. General, you can stick it up your ass. A capable artillery officer and with suitably unscrupulous conscience to shell civilian targets and aid from a well-tuned propaganda machine was what gave the victory there." And finally, "more fuel and foreign advisors than RSK and the Serbs." Now, those are the entries in your diary concerning this issue with the CALOs and the accommodations for the ECMM in Knin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And in your entries there, you say meetings with CALOs. You never actually met with General Gotovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing in these entries saying that you met with General Gotovina and that the CALO told you that you were crazy to respond to him that way because he held life and death in his hands; correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This touches on another issue whether I use my diary as an entire stenographic reproduction of every word mentioned in the whole day. I don't. What you can see in the diary, to respond to your first question, is that I have a meeting on 2nd of September. Now, at that point in time it had become an issue whether we could keep our accommodation or not, so prior to the 2nd of September we have had that issue boiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then if you could direct me again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I know this is unprecedented for me to stand but I'm the last guy to go here. I would ask the Court to please ask this gentleman to answer the question because if he is going to continue to answer like this, I'm not going to go till next week. So, I would like this person to answer the questions that Mr. Misetic is posing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, the last question was whether we can see something in this diary. You could just answer that question by saying whether we see it or whether we do not see it. You are not an accused here. There's no reason to defend even if sometimes the language might sound a bit as if someone was blaming you for something, but please focus on the questions and your answers. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, we have already tendered into evidence, Mr. Liborius, the entry from your notebook on the 6th where you noted that at a briefing -- and I believe it is in your witness statement from this past weekend, that -- here, let me find it. Yes, paragraph 13 of your last witness statement from September 2008. You referred to the fact that your notebook does have a note about an UN Sector South headquarters staff meeting, that is P802, held on 6 September, where you were informed that there had been a meeting between the UN Sector South commander and General Gotovina and that General Gotovina had apparently said there was sufficient material for a case in court against Alun Roberts. Now, you felt that sufficiently important to include it in your notebook. You didn't feel it sufficiently important to include a -- what could be construed as a threat to your physical safety by a CALO after an alleged argument with General Gotovina, and I'd like to ask you why?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid that it will develop into somewhat of a detailed answer. As I take the question that it centres on how my note taking is done, why, and when and for what purpose. Before I engage in that answer, I would seek your counsel or ask your advice on how the question should be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's okay. I will move on. Let's keep moving to get as many facts in as we can, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Just one comment also to what my friend Mr. Kuzmanovic said. If a witness is confronted it did not happen what he explained, let's be fair and give him a chance to explain and not just by answering yes or no. I think we have to be realistic and respectful of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand Mr. Misetic to move on, because what he did is to put emphasis on something that came into his mind, whether a matter was important enough. Of course you can say no, or yes. That doesn't change that much perhaps because if suddenly we said, no, it was important enough but it isn't this reason I didn't write it down, then of course we would have an explanation. If something of that kind comes to your mind, of course, Mr. Liborius, give us an explanation. But if Mr. Misetic is mainly seeking to your confirmation that you didn't write something down Mr. Misetic would expect you to have written down, then, of course it is, well, I would say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm very well comfortable with the fact that Mr. Misetic would like me to have written a lot of things down, but I decide what is necessary to support my memory when I'm monitoring and working in ECMM. I have my colleagues, I have my different reporting formats, I have my loads of papers I should produce for ECMM. And if there arises a doubt whether, first of all, as I heard earlier, that this was a -- a true reflection of what was said in the meetings, or what is said in my diary, I have to bring it to the attention of -- of the Court here that what I wrote down was in my notebooks for the meetings. The ongoing issues of housekeeping I did not have to write everything down and I do think that all sensible people will have a recollection of what happens in their immediate daily life. The fact that something is not there in my notes or my diary is not to suggest that it never take place and that was, I think, the gist of Mr. Misetic's first question. I will follow, of course, your advise to answer as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just following up on that, Mr. Liborius, you had this meeting with the CALOs in your capacity as an ECMM representative, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It was your obligation as an ECMM representative that if had you been threatened directly or indirectly by the commander of the Split Military District, in your capacity as an ECMM representative you had a duty to report that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was a direct threat at gunpoint to me, I would report it. If people said, You know you shouldn't be driving on that road because you may enter a mine, that was a frequent threat to us during the Krajina years, and in a wartime environment you do come across people who uses threats or the perception that something can be a threat as a tool in their everyday conversation and everyday conversations are not always reported in -- in the ECMM format.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's put aside the substance of the conversation. If you have a meeting with the commander of the Split Military District regardless of the topic, you had an obligation, at the end of the day when preparing your daily reports to note you had a meeting with the commander of the Split Military District, correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. If the issue was, for example, on accommodation as you started out with, and it had become a topic that we would return to, if you ask me if I had an obligation to report that in the ECMM reports, the team reports would, for housekeeping issues like this that develops, only be reported when the team felt it important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Liborius, on the 7th of September you talk about the fact that the Croatians had more fuel and foreign advisors than RSK and the Serbs. Who are the foreign advisors?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would believe that, among others, also US personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What type of assistance did the US personnel provide such that they assisted in "giving the victory" here?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would reckon that part of their advice was military advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And what about Operation Storm led to you believe that it was conducted with the advice of foreign advisors?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, the development of the Croatian army from the basis of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army and the introduction of a mobile warfare, that whole concept required military advice at a level I don't think that the Croatian army, at that time, could produce itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I'd like to tender the entire diary which I will be making reference to throughout the cross-examination. It is 1D50-0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, you also referred to 1D50-0069 as the 2nd of September entry. The note I just passed to the registrar is whether there are different numbers ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The confusion is I referred to the handwritten page of the diary instead of the translated -- transcribed version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now I see that the numbering in the translation is different from the numbering in the original. Mr. Waespi, no objections against the diary. Madam Registrar, that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D741.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D741 is admitted into evidence. I actually was looking to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is good that you assist me. We will have break and we resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if I may have 1D50-0071.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And while that is coming up on the screen, Mr. Liborius, if I could ask you were there any other meetings that you had with General Gotovina that are not in an ECMM daily report, your diary, or your notebook?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I believe not. I met General Gotovina only a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, at this alleged meeting where you had this altercation with General Gotovina, who else was present from the ECMM side?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the B/C/S ID is 1D50-0170. Okay. If we could turn to the next -- sorry, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, this is a letter dated 11 September 1995. It is from Claudio Dei. First, can you tell us who Claudio Dei is?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Claudio Dei is the CC, Coordination Centre, Split, chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you work with Mr. Dei?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have him as a team member. He was in the CC Split structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, since we're not very familiar with how the structure worked, were you within the structure that Mr. Dei was in?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the 11 September ... I had leave sometime in mid-September, but I know who Claudio Dei is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Based on the fact that as of 11 September 1995, Mr. Dei is writing to General Gotovina and ends his letter with: "Thank you again for your continuous cooperation which is highly appreciated," that this incident with General Gotovina and the CALO telling you that he had life and death in his hands that you didn't report that internally within ECMM either. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone within ECMM that you had received that kind of message from the CALO after having had a meeting with General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was discussed with my ECMM colleagues throughout August and the beginning of September what about our accomodation. So, yes, we did have frequent meetings on administration issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, that is not my question. My specific question is there is an allegation in your statement of 2005 that you had an altercation with General Gotovina and that after that altercation, the CALO told you that were crazy because he had life and death in his hands. My question is: Did you pass that information along internally within the ECMM structure?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that we should leave the ECMM accommodation, yes. But I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, the question appears to be whether you reported within your organisation that the words, You're crazy to do this because Mr. Gotovina is -- he is mastering life and death. He has it in his hands. Did you report that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is an answer to the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, turning back to this diary entry on the 7th and talking about this choice of words you had for General Gotovina followed by a capable artillery officer with an unscrupulous conscience to shell civilian targets and aid from a well-tuned propaganda machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This brings me to an issue, Mr. Misetic, that might come as a surprise. This same document apparently is there as a 65 ter document. There is a translation which is not exactly the same as you just quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it has -- as a matter of fact, I asked the legal officer to send an e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can explain it, Your Honour, and I had a conversation with Mr. Waespi about it. I assume what is with the 65 ter is the original CLSS translation of the diary. OTP then sent that original CLSS translation to Mr. Liborius, who then reviewed it, made changes and corrections to it, sent it back to OTP, and that's the one I was using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's not the one which at this moment uploaded as 65 ter P00 -- is it, 361 or whether I have to look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Something like that. That is not the same. Just that I know that the parties are aware of these inconsistencies. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I tender the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit D742.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D742 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, may I have P804 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, this is the daily report you filed for the 4th of August. Under section 2, you wrote, and the time here is 2203: "The RSK leadership have broadcasted message to the public that the army will continue fighting, however, the RSK Supreme Defence Council decided the evacuation to RS, Republika Srpska ..." Is that correct sir?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "... territory of elderly, women and children. Comment: This is assessed to be very difficult in light of the intensity of fighting." Mr. Liborius, could you tell us a little bit more, please, about this broadcast message?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The broadcast message was done by via radio to the RSK population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was brought to me by a transcript. I would usually hear in my OPS room radio broadcasts and in the rear, and if I would require a printout, either our interpreters or the interpreters at the UN Sector South headquarters would have the task, standing task of summarizing and producing resumes of radio broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What time of day did the first broadcast occur with this type of message?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I will have to see other documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In number 3, it says: "Knin received heavy artillery shelling during the morning. The evening has been fairly calm but renewed fighting with shelling in the entire southern part of Sector South is expected by first daylight." Is that accurate that the evening was fairly calm on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a marked decline in the shelling activity, as opposed to the heavy morning shelling. And I assessed it at that time that there was a -- a wish to, so to speak, empty the area of -- of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we can move on to section 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "Trains are seen being moved --"
